questions.q: What exact property marks the moment reconnaissance shifts from passive to active?
options: The moment traffic is sent directly to infrastructure the target owns or controls
The moment a tool is run from a command line instead of a web browser
The moment the tester starts taking written notes on findings
The moment the engagement's final report is drafted
questions.explain: Passive recon never sends anything to the target's own systems; active recon begins the instant a packet — a ping, a port scan, even a single curl — reaches infrastructure the target controls.

options: Runs a full-port scan with banner grabbing on every host in the range
Launches a known exploit against every host that responds
Grabs banners from every open port in the range without scanning ports
Runs a ping-style connectivity sweep to find which hosts in the range are up, without touching any ports
questions.explain: The -sn flag tells Nmap to skip port scanning entirely and just determine host liveness — the lightest active technique, useful for narrowing a range before deeper scanning.

questions.q: Why does a real engagement often scan the full port range with `nmap -sS -p- 10.20.30.15` instead of only the common-ports default?
options: Because the common-ports default always returns inaccurate results
Because -p- is required for the scan to be considered passive
Because an engagement shouldn't assume unusual services only run on well-known ports
Because UDP ports cannot be scanned any other way
questions.explain: A full 1-65535 scan avoids missing a service deliberately or accidentally run on a non-standard port, which the common-ports default would skip.

questions.q: What does banner grabbing (for example, `nc 10.20.30.15 22`) add beyond what a port scan already reveals?
options: It confirms which specific software and version is listening on that open port
It automatically patches the vulnerable service it connects to
It reveals the administrator's password for that service
It performs the same function as a ping sweep, just on a single host
questions.explain: A port scan only shows a port is open; banner grabbing connects and reads the version string the service volunteers, such as OpenSSH_8.9, which can later be checked against known vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Which pair of controls do real engagements use specifically to manage the risk that active recon introduces?
options: Running every scan from a personal, unlogged device and skipping the report entirely
Explicit IP/CIDR allow-lists plus rate-limited scan timing (e.g. Nmap's --scan-delay or -T2)
Disabling the target's firewall before scanning begins
Performing all scanning only through a public, uncontrolled Wi-Fi network
questions.explain: Because active recon is detectable and can disrupt production systems, engagements constrain it with defined scope boundaries (allow-listed ranges) and throttled timing templates, rather than firing an unthrottled scan at everything reachable.
